mappings.note: Tangents at the ends of a chord make equal angles with it BECAUSE the two tangent segments from their meeting point are equal, making the triangle isosceles. The engine is LO-3, not the right angle.
The proof of AB + CD = BC + DA is four applications of equal tangents, one at each vertex. The named theorem of LO-3.
AB = CD for two common tangents meeting at E, from EA = EC and EB = ED. Equal tangents applied to each circle in turn.
The 70 degrees between the tangents is converted to the central angle by the two contact right angles, then an isosceles triangle on the radii gives angle PAB. Lengths are not used.
Turns on the angle in a SEMICIRCLE being a right angle, with the tangent supplying the last step. The chord/arc angle result is the distinguishing content, so LO-4.
The quantity asked is the angle between the TANGENT PQ and the CHORD KL, reached through the isosceles triangle on two radii. Tangent-chord angle, hence LO-4 rather than the bare perpendicularity.
BE = CE for an incircle in an isosceles triangle, from AD = AF, BD = BE and CE = CF. Equal tangent segments only.
The proof that angle PTQ = 2 angle OPQ uses the right angle at P (LO-2) and the equality TP = TQ that makes triangle TPQ isosceles (LO-3). Neither alone completes it.
AQ is half the perimeter of ABC, from equal tangent segments at A, B and C with the circle touching two sides produced. Purely LO-3.
Halving the 80 degrees needs PO to bisect the angle, which follows from the equal tangents (LO-3); the right angle at A then gives angle POA (LO-2).
P bisects BC in an isosceles circumscribing triangle, proved by pairing equal tangent segments. No angle or right triangle is used.
A circumscribing rectangle must be a square, from equal tangent segments forcing adjacent sides equal. LO-3.
The statement of LO-2 itself, proved by showing every other point of the tangent lies outside the circle so OP is the shortest segment. The outcome's own theorem.
AQ equals half the perimeter, assembled from equal tangent segments at A, B and C. Same theorem as its twin earlier in the chapter, with the result stated as a sum of sides.
Duplicate of the earlier angle PTQ = 2 angle OPQ item, in figure form; again the contact right angle (LO-2) plus TP = TQ (LO-3) are both needed.
The common tangent at the point of contact bisects the other common tangent, because from its meeting point T the tangent segments to each circle are equal. LO-3 twice over.
OP equal to the diameter gives sin(angle APO) = 1/2 through the contact right angle (LO-2), and the equal tangents then make ABP equilateral rather than merely isosceles (LO-3).
Area of the kite PQOR is twice a right triangle whose legs are the radius and the tangent length; the right angle at each contact is what makes the area computable at all.
The given datum is the angle a TANGENT makes with a CHORD, and the central angle on that chord is wanted. Tangent-chord angle, so LO-4.
The right angle at B between OB and the tangent, plus an isosceles triangle on two radii, yields both requested angles. Only one tangent line is in play.
E bisects BC in an isosceles triangle with an incircle, from AF = AD, BE = BD and CE = CF. Equal tangents only.
Incircle tangent lengths AD, BE, CF recovered by setting one unknown and using equal tangents at each vertex. Standard LO-3 work.
PA = PB makes PAB isosceles and the given 135 degrees at A fixes its base angles, so the chord equals the tangent. The equal-tangents property supplies the isosceles triangle.
Tangents at the ends of a diameter are parallel because each is perpendicular to that diameter. A direct corollary of LO-2, with no second external point.

A tangent and a SECANT through the centre, with BC a diameter: the angle chase runs through the angle subtended by arc AC as well as the contact right angle. The chord/arc step is what distinguishes it, so LO-4.
